blocks.text: 1. Hit Rate

blocks.alt: A query is checked for at least one relevant result

blocks.text: NDCG closed by placing itself at the same familiar cutoff idea already used by precision and recall. Hit Rate, the fraction of queries where at least one relevant chunk was retrieved, closes out the ranking based metrics in this module with the simplest, coarsest measure of all.
It checks per query whether any relevant chunk appears at all, then averages across the evaluation set.
2. The Simplest Possible Question About Retrieval
Every metric covered so far in this module measures some degree or nuance of retrieval quality.
Hit rate instead asks the simplest possible question: did retrieval find anything useful at all?
3. Hit Rate Is Binary Per Query

blocks.alt: A hit scores 1 while a miss scores 0

blocks.text: Similar to how Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) scores reciprocal rank for a single query, a single query here scores exactly one if any relevant chunk appears, and exactly zero otherwise.
No partial credit exists for a query at the individual level.

blocks.text: 4. Hit Rate Versus Recall

blocks.alt: Hit rate checks at least one while recall checks all relevant found

blocks.text: Recall At K cares about how many of the relevant chunks were found, while hit rate only cares whether at least one was found.
Hit rate is the coarsest possible version of recall, collapsed to a single yes or no.
5. Hit Rate Versus MRR

blocks.alt: Hit rate is binary while MRR is position-aware

blocks.text: Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) cares exactly where the first relevant chunk landed, while hit rate only cares whether it landed within the cutoff at all.
Hit rate ignores position entirely, unlike MRR's graded reward for an earlier hit.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A relevant chunk at position one and a relevant chunk at position ten score the same hit rate of one, while MRR would score them very differently: 1.0 versus 0.1.

blocks.text: 6. Averaging Across Queries Is Where The Signal Lives

blocks.alt: Query 1 hit and query 2 miss average into the hit rate

blocks.text: Just as Precision At K gets averaged across many queries, a single query's hit rate is a meaningless zero or one on its own.
Averaging across a real evaluation set turns those individual zeros and ones into a meaningful system level percentage.
7. Hit Rate Sets A Floor On System Usefulness

blocks.alt: A low hit rate means the system is not useful

blocks.text: Just as high precision in Precision At K can still mean a missed answer, a low hit rate means the retrieval step is failing outright on many queries, not just imperfectly.
No amount of good generation prompting can recover an answer from zero relevant retrieved chunks.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A query with zero relevant chunks retrieved cannot be rescued by even the most carefully engineered prompt, since the generation model has nothing grounded to work with at all.

blocks.text: 8. Hit Rate Is Fast And Cheap To Compute
Just as extraction methods vary in cost, as seen in Entity Extraction, determining whether any relevant chunk appears requires far less judgment than assigning a graded relevance score.
Hit rate is one of the cheapest metrics in this module to actually compute at scale.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Hit Rate Is The Right First Metric To Check

blocks.alt: Starting a new evaluation points toward checking hit rate first

blocks.text: A first, coarse health check on a new retrieval system benefits from hit rate.
Fine tuning an already working system, by contrast, needs the finer signal of precision, recall, MRR, or NDCG.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates computing hit rate across a small evaluation set and contrasting it with recall on the same data.

code.content:
def hit_rate_for_query(retrieved_chunks, relevant_chunk_ids, k):
    # a hit is binary: 1 if any relevant chunk is in the top k, else 0
    top_k = set(retrieved_chunks[:k])
    return 1 if top_k & relevant_chunk_ids else 0

def recall_at_k(retrieved_chunks, relevant_chunk_ids, k):
    top_k = set(retrieved_chunks[:k])
    found = top_k & relevant_chunk_ids
    return len(found) / len(relevant_chunk_ids)

queries = [
    {"retrieved": ["c1", "c2", "c3"], "relevant": {"c1", "c9"}},
    {"retrieved": ["c4", "c5", "c6"], "relevant": {"c7"}},
    {"retrieved": ["c7", "c8", "c9"], "relevant": {"c8", "c9"}},
]

k = 3
hits = [hit_rate_for_query(q["retrieved"], q["relevant"], k) for q in queries]
recalls = [recall_at_k(q["retrieved"], q["relevant"], k) for q in queries]

print("Per query results:")
for i, (h, r) in enumerate(zip(hits, recalls)):
    print(f"  Query {i + 1}: hit={h}, recall={r:.2f}")

# average the per-query hits into one overall score
overall_hit_rate = sum(hits) / len(hits)
print(f"\nOverall hit rate: {overall_hit_rate:.2f}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the first query scoring a hit despite only finding one of its two relevant chunks, illustrating the coarser, binary nature of hit rate compared with recall.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Treating hit rate as a substitute for recall when the number of relevant chunks found actually matters.
Reading a single query's hit rate as meaningful on its own instead of averaging across a real set.
Skipping hit rate as a first health check and jumping straight to finer, more expensive metrics.
Assuming a good hit rate alone guarantees good final answer quality without checking generation too.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Hit rate is the fraction of queries where at least one relevant chunk was retrieved.
It asks the simplest possible question: did retrieval find anything useful at all.
A single query scores exactly one or zero, with no partial credit.
Hit rate is the coarsest version of recall, collapsed to a single yes or no per query.
Unlike MRR, hit rate ignores position entirely, only caring whether a hit occurred at all.
Averaging across a real evaluation set turns individual zeros and ones into a meaningful percentage.
A low hit rate signals retrieval failing outright, a floor no generation prompting can fix.
Hit rate is cheap to compute, making it a good first, coarse health check on a new system.
